title: Singapore AI Governance Framework 2026 — Measurement Implications for Deployers (Council of AI, 2026-10-07)
context: 2026-10-07 EAT cycle — Singapore's updated AI Governance Framework (second edition, 2025; refreshed Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI, May 2024) positions itself as the APAC reference for risk-proportionate AI oversight. This seed maps its principles to the Council of AI measurement model and identifies where Singapore's approach requires measurable evidence that most deployers cannot currently produce.
body: Singapore's approach to AI governance is distinctive: it is principle-based, voluntary, and explicitly designed to avoid prescriptive regulation while still demanding demonstrable accountability. The Model AI Governance Framework (second edition, January 2020) established four principles — explainability, fairness, safety, and accountability — and the refreshed Generative AI edition (May 2024) added specific requirements for foundation model transparency, content provenance, and incident reporting. For deployers operating in or serving Singapore's market, the governance gap is not the absence of rules but the absence of a measurement infrastructure that can prove compliance with principles. 'Fairness' is meaningless without a signed record of which fairness metric was chosen, what threshold was set, and what the observed distribution was at each measurement point. 'Safety' requires not just a policy document but a continuous measurement cadence that detects drift, adversarial degradation, and distributional shift. The Council of AI's 14-axis measurement board maps directly to Singapore's four principles: deterministic output and adversarial resilience cover 'safety'; detection and care axes cover 'fairness'; provenance and privacy cover 'accountability'; and the governance axis itself captures the explainability obligation. The critical difference between Singapore's framework and, for example, the EU AI Act is enforcement structure. Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) operates through an AI Verify programme that tests systems against measurable criteria — but the testing is voluntary and the results are self-reported. A verified measurement credential from the Council of AI provides what AI Verify currently lacks: an Ed25519-signed, append-only evidence chain that proves not just what the system's performance was at a point in time, but that no one has altered the record since. For multinational deployers, Singapore's framework serves as the APAC compliance baseline. Organisations that can produce a signed board manifest covering the four governance principles have a reusable evidence asset that satisfies both Singapore's voluntary requirements and, increasingly, the mandatory requirements of the EU AI Act and emerging regional frameworks in Japan, South Korea, and Australia. The practical recommendation for deployers targeting the Singapore market is to adopt a measurement cadence that produces signed capsules covering: (1) model fairness metrics with demographic parity and equalised odds where applicable; (2) safety boundary monitoring with adversarial test suites run at defined intervals; (3) content provenance records aligned to C2PA for generated outputs; and (4) incident logging into a containment index that is append-only and signed. These four measurement streams, frozen into a board manifest, constitute the minimum viable verified measurement credential for Singapore's governance context.
